title: Hacking Subagents Into Codex CLI — Brian John, Betterup
talk_summary: Brian John shows how to bolt Claude-Code-style subagents onto Codex CLI by having the parent agent invoke a fixed wrapper script that spawns a child `codex exec` process, writes its answer to a file, and prints it back to stdout. The main engineering content is the sandbox/permission fiddling needed to make nested Codex processes work, plus a note on the Agents Rule of Two security framing.

takeaways.what_they_do: Parent agent calls a wrapper script that launches a separate child agent process; the child burns its own tokens and only its final answer is written to a file and returned to the parent's context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: all that context got used up by the sub agent doesn't end up in your main context window

takeaways.technique: Fixed-command wrapper to avoid per-call approval
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of passing agent name and query as CLI args (which changes the command string and forces re-approval each time), the parent writes them to files and always runs the identical command.
takeaways.evidence_quote: As long as the command looks exactly the same, you only have to grant permission once.

takeaways.technique: Minimal-permission recipe for nested agent processes
takeaways.what_they_do: Documents the exact sandbox settings needed for a child agent to run inside a parent sandbox: workspace-write on both, credentials synced into the workspace, and the rollout recorder disabled because the parent blocks filesystem access outside the workspace.
Classifies an agent by three axes — untrusted input, access to sensitive data/systems, ability to change state or communicate externally — and argues you should not have all three at once.
Each subagent definition carries a reasoning effort (light/medium/high) matched to task difficulty, so trivial tasks don't pay for high reasoning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: depending on what kind of work it's doing, you can give it a light, medium, you can give it a high reasoning effort

takeaways.technique: Long timeouts for codebase-wide subagent tasks
takeaways.what_they_do: Uses a 600s timeout on subagent calls because codebase-wide tasks can run 10–20 minutes, and notes Codex runs subagents serially (no async).
takeaways.evidence_quote: it can take up to 10 minutes. I've actually seen them take longer, up to 20 minutes sometimes
takeaways.numbers: timeout 600s; observed 10–20 min for large-codebase tasks
